[Source: Military History Institute of Vietnam, The Plei Me Campaign, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1993]

<!-- id: EVT-2315 -->
*   **Aug. 4, 1965:** US aircraft bombed the area at the foot of Thanh Am Bridge (Van Dinh township, Ung Hoa district) at the very moment the Cho Dinh market session was crowdedly in progress, dropping 16 bombs that killed 47 people and wounded 42 others; a memorial stele was erected in the heart of Van Dinh central market to record this tragic event. [Source: Military History Institute of Vietnam, The Plei Me Campaign, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1993; Harold G. Moore & Joseph L. Galloway, We Were Soldiers Once... and Young, Random House, 1992]

<!-- id: EVT-2316 -->
*   **Aug. 18, 1965:** **Battle of Van Tuong (Quang Ngai):** The United States launched Operation Starlite, deploying around 9,000 Marines supported by armor, air, and naval gunfire to search and destroy the Liberation Army's 1st Regiment (Ba Gia Regiment). This was the first major ground engagement between US forces and the Liberation Army. Despite absolute superiority in firepower, the US Marines were intercepted and ambushed by approximately 2,000 Liberation Army troops utilizing fortified trenches and anti-tank weapons. Both sides claimed victory, but the battle proved that the Liberation Army could successfully engage and withstand large-scale US conventional forces, earning it the title "the Ap Bac against the US military." [Source: Nhan Dan Newspaper - Van Tuong Victory, a glorious milestone in national history, https://nhandan.vn/chien-thang-van-tuong-moc-son-choi-loi-trong-lich-su-dan-toc-post901618.html]

<!-- id: EVT-2317 -->
*   **Oct. 15, 1965:** Exactly one year after Nguyễn Văn Trỗi's martyrdom, Phan Thị Quyên presented their wedding photograph to Trần Độ (Chín Vinh), Member of the Central Office for South Vietnam and Deputy Political Commissar of the Liberation Army. [Source: 4th Army Corps, History of the 9th Division (1965 - 2005), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2318 -->
*   **Oct. 19 - Nov. 26, 1965:** **Plei Me Campaign and Battle of Ia Drang (Central Highlands):** The Liberation Army launched the Plei Me Campaign to lure and destroy US and ARVN forces. After a successful siege of the Plei Me camp (Oct 19 - 25), the US 1st Cavalry Division launched counter-operations, leading to the historic **Battle of Ia Drang (Nov 14 - 18)** at Landing Zones X-Ray and Albany. This was the first major conventional clash between the US Army and the regular forces of the Vietnam People's Army. Utilizing "grab the enemy by the belt" close-quarters combat tactics to neutralize US air and artillery superiority (including B-52 carpet bombings), the Liberation Army inflicted severe casualties on the US Cavalry battalions. The battle profoundly altered the US perception of the war, ending early optimism for a swift victory. [Source: Military Region 5 High Command, History of the People's Armed Forces of Military Region 5 (1945 - 2005), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2319 -->
*   **Nov. 2, 1965:** Norman Morrison, an American Quaker and pacifist, self-immolated in front of the Pentagon (USA) to protest the United States' involvement in the Vietnam War. He brought his one-year-old daughter Emily with him before committing the act. His ultimate sacrifice deeply moved the Vietnamese people and anti-war activists worldwide. [Source: Military Region 7 High Command, History of the Saigon - Gia Dinh Commandos (1945 - 1975), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2010]

<!-- id: EVT-2320 -->
*   **Nov. 4, 1965:** Poet To Huu visited Dong Hoi and conversed with Mother Suot. Inspired by her bravery, he composed the famous poem "Mẹ Suốt," which immortalized her image in modern Vietnamese literature. [Source: Party Central Committee, Party Documents, Vol. 26, National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2003]

<!-- id: EVT-2321 -->
*   **Nov. 14 - 18, 1965:** Senior Colonel Nguyen Huu An directly commanded the Battle of Ia Drang Valley (Pleime Campaign), the first regiment-level engagement defeating the US 1st Cavalry Division in the Central Highlands. [Source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 60 Years of Special Traditional Vietnam - Cuba Relations (1960 - 2020), National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2020]

<!-- id: EVT-2322 -->
*   **1965-1966 Dry Season:** The army and people of the South defeated the first dry-season strategic counter-offensive of the US. [Source: Ernesto Che Guevara, Message to the Tricontinental, Havana, 1967; National Political Publishing House, Hanoi]

<!-- id: EVT-2323 -->
*   **Dec. 1965:** The 12th Conference of the Party Central Committee (3rd tenure) made the strategic resolution to "defeat the US aggressors" and foresaw the strategy of "fighting while negotiating". [Source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 60 Years of Special Traditional Vietnam - Cuba Relations (1960 - 2020), National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2020]

<!-- id: EVT-2324 -->
*   **December 4, 1965:** **Metropole Hotel Bombing (Saigon):** Commando Team 67, led by Le Tan Quoc (Chin Quoc), used an explosive-laden truck to assault the Metropole Hotel at 148 Tran Hung Dao Street (District 5)—a billet for hundreds of U.S. Air Force pilots and logistics personnel. The explosion heavily damaged the building and surrounding military vehicles, inflicting over 130 casualties on American and South Vietnamese military personnel. [Source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 60 Years of Special Traditional Vietnam - Cuba Relations (1960 - 2020), National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2020]

<!-- id: EVT-2325 -->
*   **Dec. 18, 1965:** **Operation Game Warden:** The US Navy established Task Force 116, deploying river patrol boats (PBRs) and armed helicopters in Operation Game Warden to blockade waterways, interdict communications, and attack resistance bases of the Liberation Army and the people of South Vietnam across the Mekong Delta and the Rung Sac Special Zone. Confronting brutal naval interdiction, Vietnamese water commandos and local guerrillas stood fast, pioneering daring tactics that sank and damaged numerous enemy craft, effectively frustrating the US objective of controlling the waterways. [Source: Military History Institute of Vietnam, History of the Resistance War against the US (1954 - 1975), Vol. 3, National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2013; US Naval History and Heritage Command]

<!-- id: EVT-2326 -->
*   **Dec. 25, 1965:** The Dai Viet Revolutionary Party was founded. [Source: Institute of History, History of Vietnam, Vol. 11, Social Sciences Publishing House, Hanoi, 2014]

<!-- id: EVT-2327 -->
*   **1966:** Saigon commando Tran Van Lai secretly built a floating bunker in a house in Ba Chieu, serving as a reserve command post for the 1968 Tet Offensive. [Source: Military Region 7 High Command, History of the Saigon - Gia Dinh Commandos (1945 - 1975), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2010]

<!-- id: EVT-2328 -->
*   **1966:** Under the direction of H.63 intelligence commander Tu Cang (Nguyen Van Tau) to penetrate the enemy's command center, Tam Thao used her fluent English skills to secure a position as an interpreter at the Republic of Vietnam Navy Command, later becoming the private translator for Major James, US Naval Intelligence Advisor. From this critical vantage point, she gathered vital military intelligence, facility diagrams, and operational plans for the resistance. [Source: Larry Berman, Perfect Spy: The Incredible Double Life of Pham Xuan An, HarperCollins, New York, 2007; General Department II - Ministry of National Defense]

<!-- id: EVT-2329 -->
*   **1966:** Mother Suot was invited to attend the National Congress of Heroes and Emulation Fighters in Northern Vietnam. [Source: Central Committee of Vietnam Women's Union, Mother Suot - Transport Heroine, Women's Publishing House, Hanoi, 1999; Nhan Dan Newspaper]

<!-- id: EVT-2330 -->
*   **1966 - 1967:** The French Parliament passed an amnesty law (1966) for acts committed during the Indochina and Algerian wars, permanently erasing past convictions. Consequently, Georges Boudarel returned to France in 1967, commencing his academic career teaching and researching modern Vietnamese history at Denis Diderot University (Paris VII). [Source: Georges Boudarel, Memoirs of a Frenchman in the Vietminh, Editions Bernard Grasset, Paris, 1991]

<!-- id: EVT-2331 -->
*   **1966:** Luu Tan Phat, then Deputy Commander of Logistics for Military Region 8, heroically sacrificed his life while on a mission in Kien Phong (now Dong Thap). [Source: Military Region 9 High Command, History of Logistics of Military Region 9 (1945 - 2005), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2332 -->
* **1966:** Hero of the People's Armed Forces Bùi Chát (Trung đội trưởng công binh thuộc Trung đoàn 93, Đại đoàn 324) passed away. [Source: Department of Propaganda and Training, Heroes of the People's Armed Forces in the Resistance against French Colonialism, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1996]

<!-- id: EVT-2333 -->
* **1966:** Martyr Phạm Văn Hai (Đội trưởng Đội biệt động 65 nội thành Sài Gòn. Tham gia trận đánh kho bom Phú Thọ Hòa ngày 1 tháng 6 năm 1954, chỉ huy đơn vị tập kích hơn 30 trận vào các mục tiêu quân sự của Mỹ và chính quyền Việt Nam Cộng hòa. Hy sinh tại chiến trường Củ Chi năm 1966) heroically sacrificed his/her life while carrying out combat missions defending the Fatherland. [Source: Military Region 7 High Command, History of the Saigon - Gia Dinh Commandos (1945 - 1975), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2010]

<!-- id: EVT-2334 -->
*   **Jan. 2, 1966:** At a rally of over one million people in La Habana celebrating the 7th anniversary of the Cuban Revolution, Fidel Castro famously declared: "For Vietnam, Cuba is willing to give even its own blood." Following this, thousands of Cuban youth volunteered to go to Vietnam to fight. [Source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 60 Years of Special Traditional Vietnam - Cuba Relations (1960 - 2020), National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2020]

<!-- id: EVT-2335 -->
*   **Jan. 8 - Jan. 19, 1966:** The US and allied forces launched **Operation Crimp** with 12,000 troops, tanks, and B-52 support targeting the "Iron Triangle" (Cu Chi) to destroy the headquarters of the Saigon - Gia Dinh Military Zone. The revolutionary forces relied on the tunnel system to counterattack and preserve their forces. [Source: Military Region 7 High Command, History of Armed Forces in Eastern Nam Bo (1945 - 2005), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2336 -->
*   **Jan. 9, 1966:** South Korean troops conducted a raid and massacred 37 civilians in Kim Tai hamlet (Nhon Phong, Binh Dinh). [Source: Binh Dinh Provincial Party Committee, History of Binh Dinh Provincial Party Committee, Vol. 2, National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2000]

<!-- id: EVT-2337 -->
*   **Jan. 16, 1966:** President Ho Chi Minh spoke at a high-level cadre conference studying the 12th Central Committee Resolution, affirming the determination to defeat the US aggressors regardless of troop numbers. [Source: Ho Chi Minh Complete Works, Vol. 15 (1966 - 1969), National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2011, pp. 1-8]

<!-- id: EVT-2338 -->
*   **20/01/1966 (New Year's Eve of the Lunar Year of the Wood Snake):** Gifted poet Nguyễn Bính passed away suddenly in Nam Định at age 48. In 2000, he was posthumously awarded the Hồ Chí Minh Prize in Literature and Arts for his distinguished contributions to the New Poetry Movement and resistance literature. [Source: Vietnam Writers Association, Nguyen Binh - Poet of the Countryside, Literature Publishing House, Hanoi, 2000]

<!-- id: EVT-2339 -->
*   **Jan. 24 - Mar. 6, 1966:** **Operation Masher / White Wing:** The US 1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile) alongside the South Korean Tiger Division and Saigon forces conducted a brutal "search and destroy" sweep across liberated areas in Binh Dinh province. Despite devastating firepower deployed by the enemy that massacred civilians and destroyed villages, the Liberation Armed Forces and the people of Binh Dinh stubbornly held their ground, fiercely fighting back against hostile assaults, inflicting heavy casualties on invading troops, and preserving revolutionary bases. [Source: Military History Institute of Vietnam, History of the Resistance War against the US (1954 - 1975), Vol. 3, National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2013]

<!-- id: EVT-2340 -->
*   **Jan. 25, 1966:** The Saigon - Gia Dinh Military Command held a conference to summarize the battle, evaluating the great effectiveness of the tunnel system in "tunnel warfare." [Source: Military Region 7 High Command, Cu Chi Tunnels - A Wonder of Combat, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2008]

<!-- id: EVT-2341 -->
* **04/02/1966:** Martyr Luu Van Liet (commando fighter of Vinh Long town) heroically sacrificed his life during a surprise attack eliminating numerous enemy officers and troops at Le Hoa restaurant. [Source: Vinh Long Provincial Military Command, History of the People's Armed Forces of Vinh Long (1945 - 2005), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2342 -->
*   **1966 - Early 1967:** Le Thi Tuyet (Quang Tri) participated with the district armed forces in fighting sweep operations in the Xuan - Vinh cluster, eliminating two enemies. She was subsequently sent to study nursing. [Source: Quang Tri Provincial Party Committee, History of Quang Tri Provincial Party Committee, Vol. 2, National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2007]

<!-- id: EVT-2343 -->
* **08/02/1966:** Martyr Nguyen Van Quang (Deputy Squad Leader, 2nd Company, 303rd Battalion, Southwestern Main Force) heroically sacrificed his life in a counter-sweep battle at Co Tuat canal. [Source: Foreign Relations of the United States (FRUS), 1964–1968, Vol. IV, Vietnam; Institute of History, Hanoi, 2014]

<!-- id: EVT-2344 -->
*   **Feb. 9, 1966:** The Party Committee and the Command of the Saigon - Gia Dinh Military Zone directed the establishment of an "Anti-American Belt" surrounding the Dong Du base (Cu Chi). [Source: Binh Dinh Provincial Party Committee, War Crimes of US Expeditionary Forces and South Korean Mercenaries in Binh Dinh, National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2000]

<!-- id: EVT-2345 -->
*   **Feb. 12 - Mar. 17, 1966:** The South Korean Tiger Division carried out Operation Maengho 6 across Binh An commune (now Tay Vinh commune, Tay Son district, Binh Dinh province), brutally massacring 1,004 unarmed civilians across 15 hamlets. The atrocity culminated on Feb. 26, 1966, at Go Dai, where South Korean troops herded and slaughtered 380 innocent villagers (mostly women, elderly, and children) in a single day (the Go Dai Massacre). [Source: Hau Giang Provincial Military Command, History of the People's Armed Forces of Can Tho (1945 - 2005), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2346 -->
*   **Feb. 14, 1966:** South Korean troops of the Tiger Division committed the Thai Binh Massacre, brutally killing 65 unarmed civilians (mostly elderly people, women, and children) in Thai Binh village (now Canh Hoa commune, Van Canh district, Binh Dinh province). [Source: Quang Ngai Provincial Party Committee, War Crimes of the US Military and Allies in Quang Ngai, Quang Ngai Publishing House, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2347 -->
*   **Mar. 9 - 10, 1966:** The Battle of A Shau (Trận A Sầu) took place at the A Shau Special Forces Camp in the A Shau Valley (Thua Thien province). Established by the US to interdict the Ho Chi Minh Trail, the camp was defended by US Special Forces and Civilian Irregular Defense Group (CIDG) personnel. Following intense artillery bombardments and infantry assaults by the Liberation Army, combined with severe weather conditions that limited air support, the camp was overrun. US and allied forces suffered heavy casualties and were forced to evacuate on March 10, allowing the Liberation Army to secure a crucial strategic point on the supply route. [Source: Military History Institute of Vietnam, History of the Resistance War against the US (1954 - 1975), Vol. 3, National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2013]

<!-- id: EVT-2348 -->
*   **Mar. 10 - Jun. 19, 1966:** The "Central Vietnam Crisis" erupted as hundreds of thousands of citizens, Buddhist monastics, students, and ARVN I Corps soldiers in Da Nang and Hue took to the streets to protest the military junta of Nguyen Cao Ky and Nguyen Van Thieu and US intervention. The movement peaked in early June 1966 with the "Buddhist Altars in the Streets" campaign halting military vehicles and riot police. [Source: Institute of History, History of Vietnam, Vol. 11 (1954 - 1965), Social Sciences Publishing House, Hanoi, 2014]

<!-- id: EVT-2349 -->
*   **April 1, 1966:** **Victoria BOQ Bombing (Saigon):** Saigon Commandos drove an explosive-laden truck to breach and detonate a massive charge at the Victoria Bachelor Officers Quarters on Tran Hung Dao Street, housing over 200 U.S. officers. The explosion shook central Saigon, collapsing sections of the multi-story structure and destroying vehicles, killing and wounding dozens of American military personnel. [Source: Military Region 7 High Command, History of the Saigon - Gia Dinh Commandos (1945 - 1975), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2010]

<!-- id: EVT-2350 -->
* **28/05/1966:** Martyr Nguyen Van Lich (Scout Squad Leader of the Di An District Local Forces) though heavily wounded bravely used grenades to destroy enemy troops and heroically sacrificed his life. [Source: Binh Duong Provincial Military Command, History of the People's Armed Forces of Binh Duong (1945 - 2005), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2351 -->
* **28/05/1966:** Martyr Nguyen Van Lich (Scout Squad Leader of the Di An District Local Forces) though heavily wounded bravely used grenades to destroy enemy troops and heroically sacrificed his life. [Source: Binh Duong Provincial Military Command, History of the People's Armed Forces of Binh Duong (1945 - 2005), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2352 -->
* **26/06/1966:** Martyr Dong Phuoc Huyen (Squad Leader, 72nd Local Battalion of Quang Nam Province) heroically sacrificed his life during a counter-sweep battle in Quang Nam. [Source: Quang Nam Provincial Military Command, History of the People's Armed Forces of Quang Nam (1945 - 2005), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2353 -->
*   **Jul. 7 - Aug. 3, 1966:** **Operation Hastings:** US Marines and Saigon forces mobilized over 8,000 troops supported by heavy artillery and B-52 bombers in Operation Hastings, pushing into the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) in Quang Tri province to halt the advance of the 324B Division of the People's Army of Vietnam. Soldiers of the 324B Division alongside local forces mounted a resolute defense of strategic heights, repeatedly repelling enemy assaults, inflicting substantial casualties on US Marines, and frustrating the enemy's efforts to seal off the DMZ. [Source: Military History Institute of Vietnam, History of the 324th Division, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1992]

<!-- id: EVT-2354 -->
*   **Jul. 17, 1966:** President Ho Chi Minh issued the historic appeal: "Nothing is more precious than independence and freedom." [Source: Ho Chi Minh Complete Works, Vol. 15 (1966 - 1969), National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2011, pp. 130-134; Nhan Dan Newspaper, July 17, 1966]

<!-- id: EVT-2355 -->
*   **Aug. 9 - 10, 1966:** **Battle of Duc Co (Gia Lai):** A fierce night engagement occurred when the 5th Battalion, 33rd Regiment of the Liberation Army attacked a strategic base defended by the 3rd Battalion, 1st Cavalry Regiment of the South Korean Army near the Cambodian border. Utilizing massive artillery, armored support, and air strikes, the outnumbered South Korean defenders repelled the Liberation Army's assault. The battle was noted for the staggering volume of artillery and machine-gun fire deployed by US and South Korean forces to defend the perimeter. [Source: 3rd Army Corps High Command, History of the Western Highlands Front - 3rd Army Corps (1964 - 2005), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2356 -->
*   **Aug. 18 - 19, 1966:** **Battle of Long Tan (Ba Ria - Vung Tau):** In the rubber plantation near Long Tan (Dat Do district, Ba Ria - Vung Tau), the 5th Regiment (5th Division) of the Liberation Army together with local armed forces launched a fierce ambush and assault against an Australian infantry company from the Nui Dat base. In the face of intense artillery barrages and close air strikes desperately called in by US and Australian commanders, the Liberation soldiers courageously closed in for hand-to-hand combat, breaching defensive lines, inflicting severe casualties on Australian expeditionary troops, and rattling allied command in the region. [Source: Military Region 7 High Command, History of the 5th Infantry Division (1965 - 2005), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005; Australian War Memorial]

<!-- id: EVT-2357 -->
*   **Aug. 23, 1966:** Rung Sac commandos (Group 10) used sea mines to sink the 10,000-ton US military transport ship *Baton Rouge Victory* on the Long Tau River. This was the largest US military ship sunk on this river up to that point. [Source: Military Region 7 High Command, History of the 10th Rung Sac Commando Regiment (1966 - 2006), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2006]

<!-- id: EVT-2358 -->
*   **Sep. 14 - Nov. 25, 1966:** **Operation Attleboro:** The US military deployed over 22,000 troops under II Field Force (spearheaded by the 1st and 25th Infantry Divisions) in Operation Attleboro, a massive "search and destroy" sweep targeting the Dau Tieng - Tay Ninh area to destroy bases and logistics supply lines of the Liberation Army. Utilizing extensive tunnel systems, fortifications, and guerrilla tactics, the army and people of Eastern Nam Bo fought tenaciously, repelling enemy spearheads, inflicting over 3,200 casualties on US troops, and safeguarding the revolutionary base areas. [Source: Military History Institute of Vietnam, History of the Resistance War against the US (1954 - 1975), Vol. 3, National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2013]

<!-- id: EVT-2359 -->
* **25/09/1966:** Martyr Huynh Viet Thanh (Commander of Hau Thanh Commune Military Command) heroically sacrificed his life during a counter-sweep battle protecting local civilians. [Source: Soc Trang Provincial Military Command, History of the People's Armed Forces of Soc Trang (1945 - 2005), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2360 -->
* **08/10/1966:** Martyr Huynh Van Tao (Deputy Squad Leader, 2nd Company, 2nd Battalion of Long An Local Forces) heroically sacrificed his life in the assault on Tan Quy outpost. [Source: Soc Trang Provincial Military Command, History of the People's Armed Forces of Soc Trang (1945 - 2005), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2361 -->
*   **Oct. 9 - 13, 1966:** South Korean troops (Blue Dragon Brigade) massacred 180 civilians in Phuoc Binh and Dien Nien hamlets (Tinh Son, Quang Ngai). [Source: Hau Giang Provincial Military Command, History of the People's Armed Forces of Can Tho (1945 - 2005), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2362 -->
*   **Nov. 1966:** Over 30,000 workers in Havana, Cuba, held a massive rally to strongly express their solidarity with the Vietnamese people's anti-US resistance. [Source: Institute of History, History of Vietnam, Vol. 11, Social Sciences Publishing House, Hanoi, 2014]

<!-- id: EVT-2363 -->
*   **Nov. 17, 1966:** A United States military squad consisting of five soldiers, assigned to reconnoiter caves around Hill 192 in the Bong Son valley (Hoai Nhon, Binh Dinh province), plotted to kidnap, rape, and murder a young Vietnamese woman during their mission. [Source: Foreign Relations of the United States (FRUS), 1964–1968, Vol. IV, Vietnam; Military History Institute of Vietnam]

<!-- id: EVT-2364 -->
*   **Nov. 18, 1966:** The US squad entered Cat Tuong village (Phu My district, Binh Dinh) and kidnapped Phan Thi Mao, a young Vietnamese woman. She was bound, gagged, and subsequently gang-raped by four of the soldiers. One soldier, Robert M. Storeby, refused to participate and stood guard. [Source: Military Region 7 High Command, History of the Saigon - Gia Dinh Commandos (1945 - 1975), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2010]

<!-- id: EVT-2365 -->
*   **Nov. 19, 1966:** During a firefight with Viet Cong forces, PFC Steven Cabbot Thomas took Phan Thi Mao into the bushes, stabbed her multiple times, and ultimately shot her in the head with an M16 rifle. This brutal war crime became formally known as the "Hill 192 Incident". [Source: Military Region 7 High Command, History of the Saigon - Gia Dinh Commandos (1945 - 1975), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2010]

<!-- id: EVT-2366 -->
*   **1966-1967 Dry Season:** The army and people of the South defeated the second dry-season strategic counter-offensive of the US. [Source: Quang Ngai Provincial Party Committee, War Crimes of South Korean Mercenaries at Binh Hoa, Quang Ngai Publishing House, 2000]

<!-- id: EVT-2367 -->
*   **Late 1966:** The Soviet Union dispatched additional groups of military experts in missile science, defense industry, and electronic warfare to assist Vietnam in countering new and changing US air force tactics. [Source: Air Defense - Air Force Service, History of the Anti-Aircraft Troops (1953 - 2003), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2003]

<!-- id: EVT-2368 -->
*   **Dec. 3 - 6, 1966:** South Korean troops massacred over 400 civilians in Binh Hoa commune (Quang Ngai), mostly women, children, and the elderly. [Source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, History of Vietnamese Diplomacy (1945 - 2000), National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2002]

<!-- id: EVT-2369 -->
*   **December 4, 1966:** **Raid on Tan Son Nhut Air Base:** Commando Group F100, led by Banh Van Tran (Nam Vung), coordinated with regional sappers to covertly penetrate multiple barbed-wire perimeters and minefields at Tan Son Nhut Air Base. Utilizing B40 rockets and timed demolition charges, the commandos destroyed and damaged 67 aircraft, incinerated a fuel depot, and inflicted over 100 enemy casualties, delivering a devastating blow to the principal air base of U.S. and South Vietnamese forces. [Source: Ho Chi Minh City Women's Union, Life and Revolutionary Career of Comrade Le Thi Rieng, Ho Chi Minh City General Publishing House, 2007]

<!-- id: EVT-2370 -->
* **20/12/1966:** Martyr To Thi Huynh (Deputy Commander of Luong Hoa Commune Military Command, female guerrilla squad leader) heroically sacrificed her life defending the base during a counter-sweep battle. [Source: Military Region 7 High Command, History of the Saigon - Gia Dinh Commandos (1945 - 1975), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2010; Saigon Commando Weapons Cache Relic]

<!-- id: EVT-2371 -->
*   **1967:** The family of Nguyễn Văn Trỗi secretly exhumed and reinterred his remains at Văn Giáp Cemetery in District 2, Saigon, planting trees around the grave to conceal it from enemy authorities. [Source: Larry Berman, Perfect Spy: The Incredible Double Life of Pham Xuan An, HarperCollins, New York, 2007; General Department II - Ministry of National Defense]

<!-- id: EVT-2372 -->
*   **1967:** Le Thi Tuyet (Quang Tri) served as a nurse for the Hai Lang district military unit, operating secretly in ru Thi Ong and ru Tra Loc, areas considered as rear bases for guerrillas and wounded soldiers. [Source: Central Committee of Vietnam Women's Union, Mother Suot - Transport Heroine, Women's Publishing House, Hanoi, 1999; Nhan Dan Newspaper]

<!-- id: EVT-2373 -->
*   **1967:** Trinh To Tam was awarded the title Hero of the Armed Forces at age 22, holding a record 53 times earning the title "American-Killing Hero" on the Route 9 - Quang Tri battlefield. [Source: Department of Propaganda and Training, Heroes of the People's Armed Forces in the Anti-US Resistance, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1996]

<!-- id: EVT-2374 -->
*   **1967:** The memoir *"Bất khuất"* (Indomitable) by revolutionary fighter Nguyễn Đức Thuận (ghostwritten by journalist Trần Đĩnh) was first published in North Vietnam. Documenting his unflinching resilience through eight years of imprisonment and brutal torture in colonial and imperialist prisons (notably Con Dao Prison), the book became a profound literary-historical sensation and a symbol of the unyielding spirit of Vietnamese revolutionaries. [Source: Vietnam Women's Union, Portraits of Heroic Vietnamese Women, Women's Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2375 -->
*   **1967:** After being released from Saigon regime imprisonment, Tran Thi Quang Man was awarded the title of Hero of the Liberation Armed Forces, joined the Southern Heroes Delegation traveling to the North, and met with President Ho Chi Minh. [Source: Vietnam Women's Union, Portraits of Heroic Vietnamese Women, Women's Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2376 -->
* **1967:** Hero of the People's Armed Forces Nguyễn Quốc Trị (Thượng tá, khi tuyên dương là Đại đội trưởng bộ binh thuộc Trung đoàn 102, Đại đoàn 308, người kéo quốc kỳ trong ngày Giải phóng Thủ đô, Trung đoàn trưởng Trung đoàn Thủ Đô (1954)) passed away. [Source: Department of Propaganda and Training, Heroes of the People's Armed Forces, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1996]

<!-- id: EVT-2377 -->
* **1967:** Martyr Nguyễn Văn Quỳ (Đại đội phó bộ đội địa phương huyện Nhà Bè. Tham gia chiến đấu 24 trận cùng đơn vị diệt 149 tên, bắt sống 15 tên, thu 59 súng và nhiều máy móc, tài liệu. Hy sinh khi chiến đấu chống trận càn Cedar Falls vào vùng "Tam giác sắt" năm 1967) heroically sacrificed his/her life while carrying out combat missions defending the Fatherland. [Source: Department of Propaganda and Training, Heroes of the People's Armed Forces, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1996]

<!-- id: EVT-2378 -->
* **1967:** Hero of the People's Armed Forces Hồ Hảo Hớn (Bí thư Thành Đoàn đầu tiên của Sài Gòn - Gia Định) passed away. [Source: Air Defense - Air Force Service, History of the Vietnam People's Air Force (1955 - 2015), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2015]

<!-- id: EVT-2379 -->
* **1967:** Martyr Trần Kim Chiến (Liệt sĩ, nguyên Phó trưởng ty Công an Lào Cai. Hy sinh tháng 8 năm 1967 tại xã Phan Thanh, huyện Phan Lý Chàm (nay là huyện Bắc Bình), tỉnh Bình Thuận) heroically sacrificed his/her life while carrying out combat missions defending the Fatherland. [Source: Thua Thien Hue Provincial Party Committee, History of Thua Thien Hue Provincial Party Committee, Vol. 2, National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2380 -->
*   **1967:** Poet Xuân Quỳnh composed the immortal lyric poem *Sóng* (Waves) at Diêm Điền beach (Thái Thụy, Thái Bình) amidst the escalation of US bombing in North Vietnam. The work rapidly became one of the most cherished love poetry masterpieces in modern Vietnamese literature. [Source: Ho Chi Minh City Youth Union, Shining Examples of Uncle Ho's Generation of Youth Union Members, Tre Publishing House, 2000]

<!-- id: EVT-2381 -->
*   **Jan. 1967:** The 13th Conference of the Party Central Committee (3rd tenure) decided to step up the diplomatic struggle, opening up a "fighting while negotiating" situation. [Source: Ben Tre Women's Union, The Long-Haired Army of Ben Tre in the Anti-US Resistance, Ben Tre Publishing House, 2000]

<!-- id: EVT-2382 -->
*   **Jan. 1, 1967:** President Ho Chi Minh signed Order No. 01-LCT conferring and posthumously conferring the titles of Hero of Labor and Hero of the People's Armed Forces on outstanding collectives and individuals; awarding the title of Hero of Labor to Professor Dr. Lương Định Của (renowned agricultural scientist, breeder of high-yield rice varieties such as Nông nghiệp 1) and Mrs. Nguyễn Thị Suốt (Mother Suốt - Labor Hero in transportation, who courageously ferried troops and munitions across the Nhật Lệ River under heavy US air strikes); and conferring the title of Hero of the People's Armed Forces upon 40 outstanding officers, soldiers, and militiamen: MiG-17 fighter ace Nguyễn Văn Bảy (who shot down 7 US aircraft; later Colonel, Deputy Chief of Staff of the Air Defense - Air Force Service), Trần Hanh (Major, Deputy Commander of Air Regiment 921, distinguished in air combat defending Hàm Rồng Bridge; later Lieutenant General, Deputy Minister of National Defense), Lâm Văn Lích (fighter pilot in Regiment 923, who downed 2 US AD-6 aircraft with a MiG-17 in under 2 minutes during night combat), Thái Văn A (lookout observer on Cồn Cỏ Island, who held his observation post to guide the downing of 20 US aircraft and mark unexploded ordnance), Nguyễn Văn Mật (14.5mm anti-aircraft gun squad leader defending Cồn Cỏ), Cao Văn Khang (engineer deputy platoon leader on Cồn Cỏ Island who safely cleared unexploded bombs and recovered tons of explosives), Nguyễn Hữu Ngoãn (anti-aircraft gunner defending Cẩm Ly Dam, Quảng Bình), Dương Chí Uyển (deputy political commissar of Anti-Aircraft Battalion 71 Hà Tĩnh, Mount Nài battle), Hoàng Ngọc Chương (14.5mm anti-aircraft deputy platoon leader in Division 330), Nguyễn Tuyên (missile assembly technical team leader in Regiment 236), Hoàng Văn Nghiên (engineer platoon leader in Regiment 98, Group 559), Nông Văn Việt (engineer platoon leader in Division 7, specialized in mine clearance), Đặng Văn Thanh (political commissar in naval Group 125, captain of wooden Vessel 41 opening the sea route to Bà Rịa in 1963), Hồ Đức Thắng (naval political commissar in Group 125, commanding 16 successful unnumbered ship voyages transporting over 1,000 tons of weapons to South Vietnam), Trần Ngọc Thái (slipway team leader at naval Shipyard X.46), Trần Minh Khâm (political commissar of Transport Truck Company 1, Battalion 52, Group 559), Nguyễn Viết Sinh (porter soldier in Group 559, who carried over 55 tons of cargo on foot over 41,025 km, equal to the Earth's equator circumference), Đỗ Trực (commander of the Hồng Hà motorboat unit, Department of Transportation), Hoàng Văn Vịnh and Đỗ Văn Trì (soldiers of Division 316 defending Hill H3Q6 in Laos), Trần Ngọc Phương (soldier in Brigade 335, Phu Ba battle in Upper Laos), Đèo Văn Khổ (Battalion 51 Northwest, defending Phu Cut and Muong Ngan peaks), Hà Văn Kẹp (reconnaissance deputy platoon leader in Group 959 in Laos, Noong Khang post raid), Mùa A Páo (volunteer cadre in Laos who persuaded 300 bandits to surrender; later Colonel, Deputy Commander of Lai Châu Military Command), Phạm Hữu Thoan (postal signal squad leader, Signal Department), Major General Military Doctor Phạm Gia Triệu (Deputy Director of Military Hospital 108, pioneer who founded Vietnam's military neurosurgery), Ngô Thị Tuyển (Nam Ngạn - Hàm Rồng militiawoman who shouldered two ammunition boxes weighing 98 kg despite her 42 kg body weight to supply artillery crews), Trần Thị Lý (Đồng Hới militiawoman defending Cầu Dài bridge), Lê Văn Ban (militia platoon leader in Vĩnh Giang supplying Cồn Cỏ Island), Lê Đăng Tới (Quỳnh Vinh militia platoon leader defending Hoàng Mai railway station), Lý A Coỏng (commune military commissar of Thanh Y who dismantled armed counter-revolutionary networks), Giàng Lao Pà (commune military commander of Sín Hồ Sán, who persuaded 606 bandits to surrender), Sùng Dúng Lù (commune military leader of Vần Chải, Đồng Văn), Đặng Văn Đài (Director of Vehicle Repair Workshop X46, Military Region 4), Nguyễn Văn Dậu (technical team leader at Factory Z.2, Ordnance Department), Trương Chí Cương (reconnaissance team leader in Vĩnh Linh Armed Public Security), Nguyễn Đình Thử (border guard at Sốp Cộp post maintaining border defense with Laos), Trần Văn Nhỏ (platoon leader in Regiment 600 guarding Party and Government headquarters), and Phạm Bá Hạt (Roòn border guard post, fought 35 battles against enemy commandos and aircraft; later Colonel, Commander of Quảng Bình Border Guard); and posthumously conferring the title of Hero of the People's Armed Forces on Second Lieutenant Nguyễn Viết Xuân (anti-aircraft artillery company political commissar, who fell over Quảng Bình with the immortal cry: "Aim straight at the enemy, fire!"). [Source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 60 Years of Special Traditional Vietnam - Cuba Relations (1960 - 2020), National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2020]

<!-- id: EVT-2383 -->
*   **Jan. 8 - 26, 1967:** The US military committed 30,000 troops to Operation **Cedar Falls** in the "Iron Triangle" (Cu Chi - Ben Cat). US forces employed giant Rome Plow bulldozers and extensive bombing to completely obliterate the village of Ben Suc, burning homes and crops, forcibly deporting over 6,000 villagers into refugee camps, and declaring the area a "free-fire zone". After 18 days and nights of fierce resistance, revolutionary forces defeated the sweep, securely defending the base area. [Source: Quang Tri Provincial Party Committee, History of Quang Tri Provincial Party Committee, Vol. 2, National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2007]

<!-- id: EVT-2384 -->
*   **Jan. 27, 1967:** The Politburo issued Resolution No. 155-NQ/TW on stepping up the diplomatic struggle, actively attacking the enemy, and coordinating with military and political struggles. [Source: Military History Institute of Vietnam, History of the Resistance War against the US (1954 - 1975), Vol. 3, National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2013]

<!-- id: EVT-2385 -->
*   **Jan. 28, 1967:** Foreign Minister Nguyen Duy Trinh declared: "After the US unconditionally stops the bombing... talks with the US can be held." [Source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, History of Vietnamese Diplomacy (1945 - 2000), National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2002; Nhan Dan Newspaper]

<!-- id: EVT-2386 -->
*   **Jan. 31 - Feb. 1, 1967:** The Thủy Bồ incident (Thủy Bồ massacre) occurred in Thủy Bồ hamlet (Điện Thọ commune, Điện Bàn district, now Điện Bàn town, Quảng Nam province). During a sweep operation, US Marines (Company H, 2nd Battalion, 1st Marines) tossed grenades into bomb shelters, torched homes, and massacred 145 unarmed civilians—predominantly women, the elderly, and children—just before the Lunar New Year. In 1977, local authorities and residents erected a memorial monument commemorating the victims of the war crime (featuring the poignant sculpture of a fallen mother sheltering her surviving nursing infant). [Source: Military History Institute of Vietnam, Defeating Operation Junction City, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1982]

<!-- id: EVT-2387 -->
*   **Feb. 22 - May 14, 1967:** **Operation Junction City:** The US military committed over 30,000 expeditionary troops, thousands of armored vehicles, and hundreds of aircraft in Operation Junction City—the largest ground sweep operation of the war—striking War Zone C (Tay Ninh province) to annihilate the Central Office for South Vietnam (COSVN) and the Liberation Army Command. Standing firm with unyielding resolve, the army and people of War Zone C waged people's forest warfare for 81 days and nights, putting thousands of enemy troops out of action, destroying hundreds of aircraft and armored fighting vehicles, safeguarding leadership organs completely, and thoroughly crushing this major US strategic offensive. [Source: Vietnam People's Navy Service, History of the Vietnam People's Navy (1955 - 2015), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2015]

<!-- id: EVT-2388 -->
*   **Mar. 1967:** Captain Pham Van Dinh (Republic of Vietnam), Commander of the 52nd Battalion and District Chief of Quang Dien, secretly used his position to protect a captured Viet Cong cadre named Ky from torture and facilitated his escape. [Source: Hau Giang Provincial Military Command, History of the People's Armed Forces of Can Tho (1945 - 2005), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2389 -->
*   **May 9, 1967:** Protesters held a vigil for Norman Morrison in the United States, which culminated in a four-day occupation of the Pentagon to protest the Vietnam War. [Source: Ho Chi Minh Complete Works, Vol. 15 (1966 - 1969), National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2011, pp. 301-304; Nhan Dan Newspaper]

<!-- id: EVT-2390 -->
*   **May 9, 1967:** Betrayed by an informant, Le Thi Rieng was arrested by secret police near Da Kao market (Saigon). Despite suffering brutal torture by the CIA and the Saigon regime, she remained fiercely loyal to the revolution. [Source: Foreign Relations of the United States (FRUS), 1964–1968, Vol. V, Vietnam; Institute of History]

<!-- id: EVT-2391 -->
*   **May 16, 1967:** Buddhist nun **Nhat Chi Mai** self-immolated at Tu Nghiem Pagoda (Saigon) to pray for peace. [Source: 1967 Constitution of the Republic of Vietnam; Institute of History, History of Vietnam, Vol. 11, Social Sciences Publishing House, Hanoi, 2014]

<!-- id: EVT-2392 -->
*   **June 23, 1967:** The Democratic Republic of Vietnam and the Kingdom of Cambodia formally established diplomatic relations at the ambassadorial level. The Royal Government of Cambodia led by Head of State Norodom Sihanouk recognized and respected the territorial integrity of Vietnam within its current borders. [Source: Tom Wells, The War Within: America's Battle over Vietnam, University of California Press, 1994; Nhan Dan Newspaper]

<!-- id: EVT-2393 -->
*   **Jul. 6, 1967:** Senior General Nguyen Chi Thanh passed away suddenly in Hanoi from a heart attack at the age of 53, just prior to his scheduled return to the southern battlefield to direct preparations for the 1968 Tet Offensive. His passing was a monumental loss to the Party, the Army, and the Vietnamese people. [Source: Nhan Dan Newspaper - General Nguyen Chi Thanh: "The guerrilla general" with strategic thinking, https://special.nhandan.vn/vi-tuong-du-kich-voi-tu-duy-chien-luoc/index.html]

<!-- id: EVT-2394 -->
*   **Jul. 24, 1967:** President Ho Chi Minh received Raymond Aubrac (a French friend from 1946) and biologist Herbert Marcovic at the Presidential Palace in Hanoi. The two visitors carried a goodwill mission to mediate relations between Washington and Hanoi. Ho Chi Minh conveyed a clear message that negotiations could only occur if the US completely ceased its bombing of North Vietnam. [Source: Bertrand Russell Peace Foundation, Against the Crime of Silence: Proceedings of the Russell International War Crimes Tribunal, London, 1968]

<!-- id: EVT-2395 -->
* **28/07/1967:** Martyr Pham Van Coi (Commander of Nhuan Duc Commune Military Command, Cu Chi District, credited with destroying 120 US troops and 8 vehicles) heroically sacrificed his life in a counter-sweep battle in Cu Chi. [Source: Military History Institute of Vietnam, History of the Route 9 - North Quang Tri Front (1966 - 1973), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2002]

<!-- id: EVT-2396 -->
*   **Aug. 8, 1967:** The Government of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam issued Decision No. 121/QD-CP, reaffirming that the legal time of North Vietnam is international time zone 7, effective from January 1, 1968. [Source: Institute of History, History of Vietnam, Vol. 11, Social Sciences Publishing House, Hanoi, 2014]

<!-- id: EVT-2397 -->
* **17/08/1967:** Martyr Tran Huyen (Deputy Commander of Company 2, 74th Battalion, Intelligence Department, General Staff) heroically sacrificed his life at Con Tien - Doc Mieu base (Quang Tri). [Source: Central Committee of the Fatherland Front, The National Liberation Front of South Vietnam (1960 - 1977), National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2010]

<!-- id: EVT-2398 -->
*   **Sep. 17, 1967:** At the 2nd Heroes and Emulation Fighters Congress of South Vietnam, the National Liberation Front bestowed the title "Cu Chi, Iron and Bronze Citadel" honoring the steadfast combat spirit of Cu Chi's people; and conferred and posthumously conferred the title of Liberation Hero of the People's Armed Forces on 42 outstanding cadres and fighters; conferring upon 34 comrades: Huỳnh Thúc Bá (medic in Company 1, Battalion 72 Quảng Nam), Nguyễn Văn Bé (deputy commander of Company 304, Phú Lợi Battalion, Thủ Dầu Một), Nguyễn Ngọc Bình (deputy commander of Sapper Battalion 409, Military Region 5), Lê Văn Bảng (local company commander in Bình Thuận, single-handedly capturing or killing 56 enemies), Đoàn Văn Chia (local deputy company commander in Cần Thơ, innovator of makeshift weapons), Phan Thanh Chung (deputy platoon leader in Sapper Team 10 Quảng Trị), Bông Văn Dĩa (deputy commander of maritime Group 962 on the Sea Ho Chi Minh Trail), Hồ Dục (deputy platoon leader at Central Waystation, Western Highlands Front, transporting munitions), Đặng Văn Đâu (platoon leader in Division 5 Eastern Cochinchina), Trần Văn Đình (sapper deputy commander in Division 2 Military Region 5, Ba Gia victory), Tô Văn Đực (Cu Chi "Tank-killer Hero", creator of sweep-mines and weapon modifications targeting armored vehicles), Nguyễn Thị Hạnh (guerrilla platoon leader in Mỹ Hạnh commune, directing hundreds of engagements), Trương Văn Hòa ("US-killing Master", Điện Hòa military commander and Điện Bàn deputy commander), Lý Văn Lâm (deputy guerrilla platoon leader in Lợi An, heroically resisted an enemy ambush), Nguyễn Văn Lên (sapper reconnaissance platoon leader in Tân Uyên, four-time elite US-killer), Hồ Kan Lịch (first female hero of the Pa Kô ethnic group, guerrilla commander in western Thừa Thiên; sister of Hero Hồ A Nun), Trần Văn Lư (doctor, head of surgical team in Division 5), Đoàn Hoàng Minh (signal platoon leader in Eastern Cochinchina), Nguyễn Văn Mốt (deputy platoon leader in Group 149 Regional Logistics), Nguyễn Đức Nghĩa (deputy platoon leader in Regiment 16, Chà Dơ battle), Phạm Đình Nghiệp (deputy commander of Sapper Company 506A Quảng Ngãi, fought 30 battles, capturing or killing 79 enemies), Đinh Nghít (deputy platoon leader in Battalion 20 Military Region 5, downed a helicopter and destroyed supply trucks), Nguyễn Viết Phong (commune military leader of Mỹ Thủy, Hương Thủy, killed 112 enemy troops and destroyed 10 vehicles), Từ Văn Phước (sapper reconnaissance platoon leader in Lái Thiêu, three-time elite fighter), Nguyễn Văn Quang (heavy machine-gun squad leader in Battalion 445 Bà Rịa, killed 180 enemies and knocked out an M.41 tank), Ngô Văn Rạnh (engineer in Group 149 Regional Logistics, cleared 29 jungle tracks spanning 200 km and erected 55 bridges), Nguyễn Văn Tăng (Tư Tăng - Saigon Commando cluster commander who defended Rạch Chiếc Bridge in 1975; later Colonel), Ngô Lê Tân (chief of Signal Workshop Military Region 5), Lê Thị Thanh (Điện Hòa deputy military commander, leading political and armed struggles), Nguyễn Văn Thế (local squad leader in Long An, fought 26 battles), Nguyễn Công Tòng (company commander in Division 3 Sao Vàng in the Central Highlands), Ngô Thanh Trang (guerrilla platoon leader in Bình Đông on the Chu Lai defense belt), Tạ Quang Tỷ (commander of Battalion 4, Regiment 2, Division 9, Bình Giã campaign; later Deputy Chief of Staff of Corps 4), and Thanh Minh Tám (A Núk - sapper deputy company commander in Gia Lai, Pleiku airbase raid in 1965); and posthumously conferring upon 8 staunch martyrs: Phạm Văn Cội (Nhuận Đức military leader, Cu Chi, killed 120 US troops and 8 vehicles; sacrificed on July 28, 1967), Đồng Phước Huyến (squad leader in Battalion 72 Quảng Nam, fought 53 battles; fell on June 26, 1966), Tô Thị Huỳnh (deputy military leader of Lương Hòa, valiant female guerrilla commander; sacrificed on December 20, 1966), Lưu Văn Liệt (Vĩnh Long commando fighter, Lệ Hoa restaurant attack against US personnel; fell on February 4, 1966), Nguyễn Văn Quang (deputy squad leader in Battalion 303 Southwestern regional forces, fell at Cò Tuất canal on February 8, 1966), Huỳnh Văn Tạo (deputy squad leader in Battalion 2 Long An, fell capturing Tân Quý post on October 8, 1966), Huỳnh Việt Thanh (Hậu Thạnh commune military leader, sacrificed on September 25, 1966), and Bành Văn Trân (Saigon commando sapper, Tan Son Nhat airport raid in 1966, exiled to Côn Đảo and murdered in prison in 1968). [Source: US Department of Defense, The Pentagon Papers, Gravel Edition, Vol. 4, Beacon Press, Boston, 1971; Military History Institute of Vietnam]

<!-- id: EVT-2399 -->
*   **Sep. 29, 1967:** US President Lyndon B. Johnson declared the "San Antonio Formula," expressing willingness to stop bombing North Vietnam in exchange for productive discussions. [Source: Lyndon B. Johnson Presidential Library, Address in San Antonio, Texas, Sept. 29, 1967; Institute of History]

<!-- id: EVT-2400 -->
*   **Oct. 1967:** The Central Office for South Vietnam decided to dissolve Zone 7 and the Saigon - Gia Dinh Zone to establish the **Key Zone** (Khu Trọng điểm) consisting of Saigon - Gia Dinh and surrounding areas, divided into 6 Sub-zones to prepare for the General Offensive. [Source: Military Region 7 High Command, History of the Saigon - Gia Dinh Commandos (1945 - 1975), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2010]

<!-- id: EVT-2401 -->
*   **Oct. 17, 1967:** Battle of Ong Thanh. A clash between the 2nd Battalion, 28th Infantry Regiment (Black Lions) of the US 1st Infantry Division and forces of the Liberation Army of South Vietnam (two battalions of the 1st Regiment, 9th Division) at Ong Thanh stream (Binh Duong). The Liberation Army organized a well-prepared active defense and ambush, completely annihilating the US Alpha Company and inflicting heavy casualties on the Delta Company, resulting in 64 US officers and soldiers killed (including the battalion commander, Lt. Col. Terry Allen). The battle demonstrated the effectiveness of the Liberation Army's ambush tactics, although the US military withheld details of the battle from the public until 1991. [Source: Military History Institute of Vietnam, History of the Resistance War against the US (1954 - 1975), Vol. 3, National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2013; David Maraniss, They Marched into Sunlight, 2003]

<!-- id: EVT-2402 -->
*   **Nov. 3 - 22, 1967:** Battle of Dak To. A major direct confrontation between the Liberation Army of South Vietnam (primarily the 1st Division) and US and Republic of Vietnam forces in Kon Tum. Employing a "luring the tiger out of the mountain" tactic, the Liberation Army drew the US 173rd Airborne Brigade and 4th Infantry Division into a trap at Hill 875. Despite the US mobilizing massive air and artillery firepower (over 150,000 artillery shells and 10,000 tons of bombs), the Liberation Army utilized "mobile attack combined with fortified defense" tactics, inflicting severe casualties on elite US units. The battle proved the Liberation Army's capability to withstand and defeat modernly equipped US expeditionary forces, thwarted the enemy's campaign separation intentions, and severely depleted US manpower. [Source: 3rd Army Corps High Command, History of the Western Highlands Front - 3rd Army Corps (1964 - 2005), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2403 -->
*   **Nov. 27, 1967:** The Central Military Commission established the Command of Group 559 (Truong Son Troops Command) under Senior Colonel Dong Si Nguyen as Commander. This marked a pivotal transition shifting the Truong Son logistics route from manual methods to large-scale mechanized transport and combined-arms operations, turning the Ho Chi Minh Trail into a robust network overcoming enemy aerial interdiction. [Source: Nhan Dan Newspaper - Lieutenant General Dong Si Nguyen - Legendary Commander of the Truong Son Trail, https://nhandan.vn/special/Trung-tuong-Dong-Sy-Nguyen-Tu-lenh-Duong-Truong-Son-huyen-thoai/index.html]

<!-- id: EVT-2404 -->
* **1968:** Martyr Banh Van Tran (Saigon commando fighter who participated in the Tan Son Nhat Airport raid on Dec. 2, 1966) heroically sacrificed his life in Con Dao Prison. [Source: Ba Ria - Vung Tau Provincial Party Committee, History of Con Dao Prison (1862 - 1975), National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2002]

<!-- id: EVT-2405 -->
*   **1968:** During the Tet Offensive (Mau Than), female intelligence officer Dinh Thi Van directly guided the preparation of the "Vu Mua" (Harvest) intelligence plan in Saigon. Her network provided timely reports and secured communication routes for revolutionary forces entering the city without being detected by the enemy. [Source: General Department II - Ministry of National Defense, History of Vietnam Defense Intelligence (1945 - 2015), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2015]

<!-- id: EVT-2406 -->
* **1968:** Hero of the People's Armed Forces Bùi Ngọc Dương (quê tại Hà Nội) passed away. [Source: Department of Propaganda and Training, Heroes of the People's Armed Forces, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1996]

<!-- id: EVT-2407 -->
* **1968:** Hero of the People's Armed Forces Bế Văn Cắm (quê tại Cao Bằng) passed away. [Source: Department of Propaganda and Training, Heroes of the People's Armed Forces, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1996]

<!-- id: EVT-2408 -->
* **1968:** Hero of the People's Armed Forces Nguyễn Văn Bích (Trung đội phó Công binh đánh cầu Phân khu 1 Sài Gòn - Gia Định, chỉ huy nhiệm vụ đánh sập cầu Phú Cường (Bình Dương) năm 1968) passed away. [Source: Military Region 7 High Command, History of Armed Forces in Eastern Nam Bo (1945 - 2005), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2409 -->
* **1968:** Hero of the People's Armed Forces Nguyễn Văn Xơ (Phó Chính ủy Trung đoàn 1, Sư đoàn 9, Bộ đội miền Đông Nam Bộ, chỉ huy nhiệm vụ tấn công Trung tâm Huấn luyện Quang Trung trong chiến dịch Tổng tiến công và nổi dậy mùa Xuân 1968) passed away. [Source: 4th Army Corps, History of the 9th Division (1965 - 2005), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2410 -->
* **1968:** Hero of the People's Armed Forces Võ Văn Điều (Tiểu đoàn trưởng Tiểu đoàn 261 phá hủy 9/13 xe tăng M.13 trong trận Ấp Bắc (Mỹ Tho), được mệnh danh là "Anh hùng Ấp Bắc" (1963), sau này là Trung đoàn trưởng Trung đoàn 31 Phân khu Bắc Long An, chỉ huy quân giải phóng đánh vào Trung tâm Bưu chính Phú Lâm Quận 6 trong chiến dịch Mậu Thân 1968) passed away. [Source: 330th Division, History of the 261st Giron Battalion, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2000]

<!-- id: EVT-2411 -->
* **1968:** Hero of the People's Armed Forces Hà Văn Chúc (Phi công Không quân Nhân dân Việt Nam) passed away. [Source: Air Defense - Air Force Service, History of the Vietnam People's Air Force (1955 - 2015), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2015]

<!-- id: EVT-2412 -->
* **1968:** Martyr Trần Văn Hai (Các liệt sĩ thiếu niên Việt Nam) heroically sacrificed his/her life while carrying out combat missions defending the Fatherland. [Source: Department of Propaganda and Training, Heroes of the People's Armed Forces, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1996]

<!-- id: EVT-2413 -->
* **1968:** Hero of the People's Armed Forces Trần Văn Kiểu (Thủ lĩnh phong trào công nhân tại Nam Bộ, sau bị chính quyền VNCH thủ tiêu) passed away. [Source: Department of Propaganda and Training, Heroes of the People's Armed Forces, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1996]

<!-- id: EVT-2414 -->
* **1968:** Hero of the People's Armed Forces Lê Tấn Quốc (Chiến sĩ Biệt động Sài Gòn) passed away. [Source: Department of Propaganda and Training, Heroes of the People's Armed Forces, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1996]

<!-- id: EVT-2415 -->
* **1968:** Hero of the People's Armed Forces Hoàng Kim Giao (Thiếu úy, nghiên cứu viên Viện Kỹ thuật Quân sự) passed away. [Source: Department of Propaganda and Training, Heroes of the People's Armed Forces, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1996]

<!-- id: EVT-2416 -->
* **1968:** Martyr Huỳnh Lan Khanh (Liệt sĩ, nguyên chiến sĩ Cơ quan Trung ương Mặt trận Dân tộc giải phóng miền Nam Việt Nam. Con gái của Chủ tịch Chính phủ Cách mạng lâm thời Cộng hòa miền Nam Việt Nam Huỳnh Tấn Phát) heroically sacrificed his/her life while carrying out combat missions defending the Fatherland. [Source: Department of Propaganda and Training, Heroes of the People's Armed Forces, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1996]

<!-- id: EVT-2417 -->
*   **1968:** After graduating with distinction from MiG-21 jet fighter pilot training in the Soviet Union, pilot Vũ Xuân Thiều returned to Vietnam and was assigned to the 921st Fighter Regiment (Sao Do) and later the 927th Regiment of the 371st Air Division, actively undertaking combat standby duties to defend the airspace of North Vietnam. [Source: Department of Propaganda and Training, Heroes of the People's Armed Forces, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1996]

<!-- id: EVT-2418 -->
*   **Jan. 1968:** The 14th Conference of the Party Central Committee (3rd tenure) passed the resolution on the General Offensive and Uprising (Tet Mau Than) to deal a decisive blow to the US will of aggression. [Source: Department of Propaganda and Training, Heroes of the People's Armed Forces, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1996]

<!-- id: EVT-2419 -->
*   **January 6, 1968:** Nguyen Van Bach, the eldest son of Le Thi Tuyet (Tra Cu), joined the revolution. He later became a Platoon Leader in the 306th Battalion. [Source: Department of Propaganda and Training, Heroes of the People's Armed Forces in the Anti-US Resistance, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1996]

<!-- id: EVT-2420 -->
*   **Jan. 20 - Jul. 15, 1968:** Battle of Khe Sanh (Route 9 - Khe Sanh Campaign). The Liberation Army of South Vietnam launched a massive offensive against the US defense complex at Khe Sanh in Quang Tri. Serving as a strategic diversion for the Tet Offensive, the Liberation Army closely besieged the base (with 17,000 troops), forcing the US to deploy strategic bombers to drop over 114,000 tons of bombs for support. For the first time, the Liberation Army deployed PT-76 tanks, overrunning the Lang Vei Special Forces camp (Feb. 7). Despite casualties from intense US firepower, the campaign successfully pinned down a large US force, destroyed the command center of the McNamara Line, and ultimately forced the US military to abandon Khe Sanh in July 1968. This marked the first time the US military had to abandon a major base due to enemy pressure. [Source: Nhan Dan Newspaper - The Route 9 - Khe Sanh Victory, https://special.nhandan.vn/chien-thang-Duong9-Khe-Sanh-tran-danh-lam-nen-chien-cong-bat-tu-Tet-Mau-Than-1968-/index.html]

<!-- id: EVT-2421 -->
*   **Night of Jan. 30-31, 1968:** The 1968 Tet General Offensive and Uprising broke out simultaneously across South Vietnam, attacking cities, towns, and the enemy's command centers, shaking the US's will to aggression. [Source: https://nhandan.vn/tong-tien-cong-noi-day-xuan-mau-than-1968-sang-tao-trong-dieu-hanh-chien-tranh-cua-dang-post865087.html]

![Historical Image](images/event_20260923_125749.webp)

*Source: Sapper commandos studying a battle map in preparation for the 1968 Tet Mau Than General Offensive / Wikimedia Commons (Public domain)*

<!-- id: EVT-2422 -->
*   **Jan. 31, 1968:** During the Tet Offensive (the 2nd day of the Lunar New Year), female revolutionary Le Thi Rieng was executed by the Saigon regime at Ba Hoa post in Cho Lon. In her final moments, she used her body to shield her comrade Phung Ngoc Anh from bullets and valiantly sang the Internationale. [Source: Nhan Dan Newspaper - July days of martyr Le Thi Rieng's family, https://nhandan.vn/nhung-ngay-thang-7-cua-gia-dinh-liet-si-le-thi-rieng-post976605.html]

<!-- id: EVT-2423 -->
*   **Jan. 31, 1968:** In the early morning hours of the Tet Offensive, intelligence commander Tu Cang (Nguyen Van Tau) and female operative Tam Thao (Nguyen Thi My Nhung) witnessed the fierce assault by Commando Group 5 on the Independence Palace from an undercover base house 100 meters away. Tu Cang opened fire with his K54 pistol, killing two enemy officers to support his surrounded commando comrades. When enemy police stormed the house to search, Tam Thao calmly utilized her poise and undercover role with the US Naval Advisor to mislead them, ensuring Tu Cang's safe cover. [Source: General Department II - Ministry of National Defense, The Man Whose Legs Were Severed Six Times - Major Nguyen Van Thuong, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2005]

<!-- id: EVT-2424 -->
*   **Jan. 31 - Feb. 24, 1968:** Battle of Hue during the Tet Offensive. Commencing in the early hours of the Lunar New Year, the Liberation Army of South Vietnam launched a surprise attack and seized control of most of Hue city, raising the Front's flag over the Citadel. US and Republic of Vietnam forces mobilized massive reinforcements for a counterattack. To retake the city, the US military utilized heavy firepower (bombs and naval artillery), resulting in the severe destruction of 80% of Hue's structures and significant civilian casualties. After holding the city in fierce urban combat for 25 days, the Liberation Army proactively withdrew to preserve their forces. The battle dealt a colossal psychological and political blow to the United States, demonstrating the Liberation Army's ability to hold a major city for an extended period. [Source: Nhan Dan Newspaper - Tet Offensive Assault in Hue, https://special.nhandan.vn/tran-tien-cong-Tet-Mau-Than/index.html]

<!-- id: EVT-2425 -->
*   **January 31, 1968:** **Attack on the Saigon National Radio Station:** At 02:00 on the second day of the Lunar New Year (Tet Mau Than), 11 fighters of Saigon Commando Team 4, led by Nguyen Gia Loc (Nam Loc), launched a surprise assault in two vehicles on the Saigon National Radio Station (Radio Saigon, No. 3 Phan Dinh Phung Street). Blasting through the gate and neutralizing guards, they captured the entire facility within 15 minutes with the objective of broadcasting a pre-recorded call for a General Uprising from the National Liberation Front. However, South Vietnamese authorities immediately cut the transmitter link at the Phu Tho relay station, while deploying paratroopers, military police, and armored cars in a fierce counterattack. Completely isolated without reinforcements, Team 4 fought courageously for hours; upon exhausting their ammunition, the commandos detonated explosives to destroy the broadcasting equipment and heroically sacrificed their lives. [Source: Nhan Dan Newspaper - Saigon Commandos: Special armed forces, https://thongnhatdatnuoc.nhandan.vn/biet-dong-sai-gon-luc-luong-vu-trang-dac-biet-642.html]

<!-- id: EVT-2426 -->
*   **January 31, 1968:** **Attack on the U.S. Embassy in Saigon:** In the early morning of Tet Mau Than, 19 fighters of Saigon Commando Team 11, commanded by Ngo Thanh Van (Ba Den) and political commissar Ta Van Pham (Ut Nho), approached the fortified U.S. Embassy on Thong Nhut Boulevard. Using C4 explosives to breach the perimeter wall, they eliminated security guards and secured the ground floor and grounds of the compound. For six hours, the commandos fiercely resisted counterattacks by the U.S. 716th Military Police Battalion and 101st Airborne Division paratroopers landing on the chancery roof by helicopter. Fifteen commandos fell in combat after inflicting significant American casualties. The assault on America's diplomatic stronghold in Saigon was broadcast globally, dispelling claims of wartime progress and dealing a decisive blow to American public support for the war. [Source: Government News Portal - Strategic Leadership of the Party in the 1968 Tet Offensive, https://baochinhphu.vn/su-chi-dao-chien-luoc-cua-dang-trong-cuoc-tong-tien-cong-va-noi-day-mau-than-1968-10223020118390215.htm]

<!-- id: EVT-2427 -->
*   **January 31 - February 1, 1968:** **Attack on the Independence Palace:** In the early hours of January 31, 1968, 15 fighters of Saigon Commando Team 5 (14 men and female fighter Vu Minh Nghia), led by To Hoai Thanh (Ba Thanh), launched an assault on the rear gate of the Independence Palace (Nguyen Du Street), staging from Hero Tran Van Lai's secret weapons depot at 287/70 Phan Dinh Phung Street. When their primary demolition charge failed against the iron gate, the team engaged guard posts with B40 rockets and automatic weapons, inflicting heavy casualties on presidential guards. Confronting overwhelming fire from armored vehicles, Team 5 withdrew to an unfinished building at 56 Thu Khoa Huan Street, fortifying upper floors and holding off dozens of enemy counterattacks for nearly two days and nights. Exhausting their ammunition, seven commandos (including commander Ba Thanh) were killed in action, and the remaining wounded fighters were captured. [Source: https://nhandan.vn/biet-dong-thanh-chien-cong-nhu-huyen-thoai-post314935.html]

![Historical Image](images/event_20260923_225156.webp)

*Source: The Independence Palace, Saigon, Mar. 1969 / Wikimedia Commons (Public domain)*

<!-- id: EVT-2428 -->
*   **January 31 - February 1, 1968:** **Attack on the South Vietnamese Joint General Staff Compound:** In the early hours of January 31, 1968, fighters of Saigon Commando Team 6, cooperating with the 2nd Go Mon Battalion, mounted a fierce assault against Gates 4 and 5 of the Republic of Vietnam Joint General Staff (JGS) Compound on Vo Di Nguy and Vo Tanh Streets. Utilizing demolition charges and B40 rockets, the assault force breached sentry gates and captured several administrative buildings. They held their ground against repeated counterattacks by headquarters defense battalions, military police, and armor, ambushing a convoy of U.S. military police reinforcements and inflicting heavy losses before maneuvering into adjoining urban areas. [Source: Ho Chi Minh City Youth Union, Shining Examples of Uncle Ho's Generation of Youth Union Members, Tre Publishing House, 2000]

<!-- id: EVT-2429 -->
*   **January 31, 1968:** **Attack on the South Vietnamese Naval Headquarters:** In the early hours of Tet Mau Than, 16 fighters of Saigon Commando Team 3, commanded by Nguyen Van Lap (Ba Lap), approached and attacked the Republic of Vietnam Navy Headquarters at Bach Dang Quay in two vehicles. Overrunning an outer security checkpoint at Me Linh Square, the commandos fired B40 rockets and stormed the main entrance. Encircled by heavy machine guns, South Vietnamese naval forces, and U.S. military police, Team 3 resisted tenaciously to the last bullet, with most fighters sacrificing their lives on the compound grounds. [Source: Ben Tre Women's Union, The Long-Haired Army of Ben Tre in the Anti-US Resistance, Ben Tre Publishing House, 2000]

<!-- id: EVT-2430 -->
*   **Feb. 1, 1968:** During the Tet Offensive, Viet Cong commando Nguyen Van Lem (alias Bay Lop) was captured in Cho Lon and summarily executed on a Saigon street by Nguyen Ngoc Loan, Chief of the South Vietnamese National Police, without trial. The moment was captured by AP photojournalist Eddie Adams in the iconic photograph *"Saigon Execution"*, as well as on film by NBC cameraman Vo Suu. The photograph won the 1969 Pulitzer Prize, becoming a worldwide symbol of the war's brutality that galvanized the anti-war movement in the United States and dramatically shifted international public opinion on the Vietnam War. [Source: People's Police Newspaper - The Fate of Nguyen Ngoc Loan: Executioner of the Tet Offensive, https://antg.cand.com.vn/Tu-lieu-antg/So-phan-cua-Sau-Leo-Nguyen-Ngoc-Loan---Dao-phu-Tet-Mau-Than-i303366/]

<!-- id: EVT-2431 -->
*   **Early 1968:** Thiều Văn Chỏi was admitted to the Communist Party of Vietnam. [Source: Quang Tri Provincial Party Committee, History of Quang Tri Provincial Party Committee, Vol. 2, National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2007]

<!-- id: EVT-2432 -->
*   **Feb. 7, 1968:**   **Battle of Lang Vei (Route 9 - Khe Sanh Campaign):** The Liberation Army of South Vietnam launched a decisive assault to overrun the fortified Lang Vei Special Forces Camp (Huong Hoa, Quang Tri) – a vital outpost commanded by US Army Special Forces (Green Berets - Detachment A-101) shielding the western approach to the Khe Sanh Combat Base. The assault force was spearheaded by the 24th Regiment (304th Division, commanded by Le Cong Phe and Political Commissar Le Tam), supported by the 3rd Battalion (101st Regiment), sappers, combat engineers, and artillery. The battle marked a historic milestone as the **first combat deployment of armor by the Vietnam People's Army** in the Vietnam War: the 198th Armored Battalion (commanded by Ha Tien Tuan) secretly marched over 1,300 km from the North to deploy 16 PT-76 amphibious light tanks. Commencing at 23:30 on the night of February 6 with preparatory artillery barrages, PT-76 tanks shocked the defenders by tearing through heavy barbed wire entanglements and crushing hardened bunkers and machine-gun nests, paving the way for infantry to penetrate the inner perimeter; notably, Tank No. 555 led by Deputy Platoon Commander Le Xuan Tau spearheaded the vanguard breakthrough. By the morning of February 7, the camp was completely overrun; over 300 enemy troops were killed and 253 captured (including US advisors), and vast quantities of arms were seized. The victory at Lang Vei shattered the enemy's western defensive shield, completely isolating Khe Sanh (Ta Con base) and establishing the legendary tradition *"Once deployed, victory is secured"* for the Vietnam Tank and Armored Corps. [Source: Ho Chi Minh Complete Works, Vol. 15 (1966 - 1969), National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2011, p. 418; Nhan Dan Newspaper]

<!-- id: EVT-2433 -->
*   **Feb. 12, 1968:** South Korean troops massacred 69-79 unarmed civilians in Phong Nhat and Phong Nhi villages (Dien Ban, Quang Nam). [Source: Military History Institute of Vietnam, The Khe Sanh - Route 9 Campaign Spring-Summer 1968, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1998]

<!-- id: EVT-2434 -->
*   **Feb. 21, 1968:** South Korean troops (Blue Dragon Brigade) massacred 135 unarmed civilians in Ha My village (Dien Ban, Quang Nam). [Source: Party Central Committee, Party Documents, Vol. 29, National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2004]

<!-- id: EVT-2435 -->
*   **Mar. 16, 1968:** The **My Lai Massacre** (Son My Massacre) occurred in Quang Ngai. US Army troops (Charlie Company) massacred 504 unarmed civilians (according to Vietnamese statistics). This event shocked the world and intensified the anti-war movement. [Source: Military History Institute of Vietnam, The 1968 Tet General Offensive and Uprising, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1998]

![Historical Image](images/event_20260924_111703.webp)

*Source: Scene of the My Lai massacre, March 16, 1968 / Ronald L. Haeberle, U.S. Army (Wikimedia Commons, Public domain)*

<!-- id: EVT-2436 -->
*   **Mar. 31, 1968:** US President Johnson announced a limited bombing halt of the North (from the 20th parallel northwards) and agreed to negotiations. [Source: Military History Institute of Vietnam, The 1968 Tet General Offensive and Uprising, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1998]

<!-- id: EVT-2437 -->
*   **Apr. 1968:** The Command of Group 559 and the General Logistics Department commenced construction of the first tactical petroleum pipeline (Route X42, 42 km from Nam Dan through Linh Cam), opening the historic feat of building the trans-Truong Son pipeline system spanning over 5,000 km that delivered hundreds of thousands of tons of fuel to southern battlefields for the liberation of the South. [Source: Military Region 7 High Command, History of the Saigon - Gia Dinh Commandos (1945 - 1975), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2010]

<!-- id: EVT-2438 -->
*   **Apr. 1 - 14, 1968:** **Operation Pegasus:** The US military launched Operation Pegasus along Route 9, deploying the 1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile) and Marine forces to relieve the suffocating siege laid by the People's Army of Vietnam around the Khe Sanh Combat Base (Quang Tri province). Confronting intense air and artillery strikes, Liberation soldiers fiercely resisted every enemy advance, downing numerous helicopters and attriting US combat strength before deliberately shifting operational axes. [Source: Military Region 7 High Command, History of the Saigon - Gia Dinh Commandos (1945 - 1975), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2010]

<!-- id: EVT-2439 -->
*   **Apr. 6 - 7, 1968:** During the defense of Hill 595 in the Route 9 - Khe Sanh Campaign, a squad of the Liberation Army of South Vietnam fiercely repelled multiple assaults by US Marines. Over the 45-day defense, which culminated in intense combat during these two days, soldier Tran Huu Bao single-handedly eliminated 78 enemy troops. [Source: Military Region 7 High Command, History of the Saigon - Gia Dinh Commandos (1945 - 1975), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2010]

<!-- id: EVT-2440 -->
*   **Apr. 19 - May 17, 1968:** **Operation Delaware:** The US military committed the 1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile) and 101st Airborne Division in massive helicopter assaults into the A Shau Valley (Thua Thien province) to sever the vital logistics hub on the Ho Chi Minh Trail. Liberation Army troops and antiaircraft gunners threw up a lethal low-altitude curtain of fire, downing and destroying dozens of sophisticated US helicopters, defeating sweeping columns, and forcing US forces to withdraw from the valley. [Source: Military Region 7 High Command, History of the Saigon - Gia Dinh Commandos (1945 - 1975), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2010]

<!-- id: EVT-2441 -->
*   **Apr. 19, 1968:** Tam Ha (Tran Van Dac), Deputy Political Commissar of the Northern Wing of the Liberation Army, surrendered to the US and Republic of Vietnam forces. He disclosed the entire plan for the second wave of the Tet Offensive, including locations of hidden artillery and rockets, causing severe damage to the revolutionary forces. [Source: Military Region 7 High Command, History of the Saigon - Gia Dinh Commandos (1945 - 1975), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2010]

<!-- id: EVT-2442 -->
*   **Apr. 20, 1968:** The Alliance of National, Democratic, and Peace Forces of Vietnam was established in the liberated zone of Tay Ninh to gather intellectuals and the urban bourgeoisie. [Source: Military History Institute of Vietnam, The 1968 Tet General Offensive and Uprising, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1998; Mark Bowden, Hue 1968, 2017]

<!-- id: EVT-2443 -->
*   **Apr. 21 - 26, 1968:** Intelligence officers Tu Cang and Pham Xuan An (H63 intelligence network) successfully obtained the highly classified confession of defector Tam Ha from the Saigon authorities. By April 26, their critical report reached the B2 Command, helping the revolutionary leadership assess the situation and resolve to proceed with the second wave of the Tet Offensive to crush the US military's will. [Source: Military History Institute of Vietnam, The 1968 Tet General Offensive and Uprising, People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 1998; Eddie Adams, Pulitzer Prize 1969]

<!-- id: EVT-2444 -->
*   **May 1968:** **Exploits of the Le Thi Rieng Female Commando Unit (The 11 Saigon Commando Girls):** During Phase 2 of the Tet Offensive, the all-female commando unit named after martyr Le Thi Rieng under Sub-region 6 (comprising 11 young women led by Le Hong Quan) boldly spearheaded assaults against key installations in downtown Saigon. The unit captured the District 5 Administrative Building and held defensive positions at Thiec Market and the Lido Cinema, beating back intense counterattacks by paratroopers, rangers, and armored units for days and nights, safeguarding critical urban corridors and becoming a legendary symbol of revolutionary courage among Saigon women. [Source: People's Army Newspaper - Southern women in the Spring 1968 Tet Offensive and Uprising, https://www.qdnd.vn/50nam-tong-tien-cong-va-noi-day-xuan-mau-than1968/danh-gia-phan-tich/phu-nu-mien-nam-trong-cuoc-tong-tien-cong-va-noi-day-xuan-mau-than-1968-530402]

<!-- id: EVT-2445 -->
*   **May 4, 1968:** The second wave of the Tet Offensive commenced in Saigon despite compromised plans. The fierce attacks dealt a massive psychological blow to the US, contributing to General William Westmoreland's dismissal and President Lyndon B. Johnson's decision not to seek re-election, pushing the US toward peace negotiations. [Source: Ho Chi Minh City Women's Union, Life and Revolutionary Career of Comrade Le Thi Rieng, Ho Chi Minh City General Publishing House, 2007; Le Thi Rieng Tomb Monument]

<!-- id: EVT-2446 -->
*   **May 13, 1968:** Official negotiations between the delegations of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam and the US began in Paris. [Source: Armored Cavalry High Command, History of the Armored Branch (1959 - 2009), People's Army Publishing House, Hanoi, 2009]

<!-- id: EVT-2447 -->
*   **July 5, 1968:** In the morning, Le Thi Tuyet (Quang Tri) was captured by the puppet 4th Marine Battalion at Ben Thi Ong and subjected to severe torture, including having soapy water mixed with chili powder poured into her mouth. In the afternoon, refusing to confess, she was tied to a jackfruit tree, brutally mutilated (her breasts and ears were cut, her abdomen opened, and her liver extracted), and buried alive up to her neck. Ten enemy soldiers sliced her liver into 11 pieces and cooked it in front of witnesses. She survived in the hole for two days and two nights before passing away. [Source: Quang Nam Provincial Party Committee, War Crimes of South Korean Mercenaries in Quang Nam, National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2000]

<!-- id: EVT-2448 -->
*   **Jul. 24, 1968:** At 16:00, 10 female Youth Volunteers belonging to Squad 4, Company 552, General Squad 55 died heroically at Dong Loc Junction (Ha Tinh). While they were sheltering in an A-shaped bunker after leveling bomb craters to ensure the traffic artery for the southern battlefield, a US bomb directly hit their position. The youngest was 17, and the three oldest were 24. Their sacrifice became an immortal epic of the Vietnamese youth's indomitable spirit. [Source: Quang Nam Provincial Party Committee, War Crimes of South Korean Mercenaries in Quang Nam, National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 2000]

<!-- id: EVT-2449 -->
*   **Aug. 1968:** The Central Office for South Vietnam decided to re-establish the Saigon - Gia Dinh City Party Committee (code name Binh Gia). The City Party Committee's base was moved to Ba Thu (border area). [Source: Walter Cronkite, Report from Vietnam: Who, What, When, Where, Why?, CBS News Special Report, Feb. 27, 1968]

<!-- id: EVT-2450 -->
*   **Aug. 2, 1968:** At the Saigon regime's Field Military Court of Tactical Zone 3, Saigon commando Vo Thi Thang was sentenced to 20 years of hard labor. Upon hearing the verdict, she indomitably smiled and boldly stated: *"Will your government survive 20 years to imprison me?"*. Captured by a Japanese photojournalist, the photograph titled *"The Smile of Victory"* became an immortal symbol of the unyielding spirit of the Vietnamese people. [Source: Quang Ngai Provincial Party Committee, The Son My Massacre (March 16, 1968), National Political Publishing House, Hanoi, 1998; Seymour Hersh, My Lai 4, Random House, 1970]

<!-- id: EVT-2451 -->
* **18/08/1968:** Martyr Vo Lai (Battalion Commander of the 52nd Local Battalion of Binh Dinh Province) heroically sacrificed his life in a battle in Binh Dinh. [Source: Lyndon B. Johnson Presidential Library, Statement Announcing General Westmoreland's Appointment as Chief of Staff, March 22, 1968]

<!-- id: EVT-2452 -->
*   **Aug. 19, 1968:** Bui Van Thuyen was officially admitted to the Communist Party of Vietnam. [Source: Clark Clifford, Counsel to the President: A Memoir, Random House, New York, 1991; Military History Institute of Vietnam]

<!-- id: EVT-2453 -->
*   **Oct. 11, 1968 (or Oct. 13, 1968):** Mother Suot heroically died in a US bombing raid near the Bao Ninh ferry crossing while carrying out a mission to transport food and supplies.
